sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer different route to language generation: reconstructing sequences through iterative denoising, with multiple tokens predicted in parallel. This formulation connects flexible generation order with the prospect of efficient inference. Progress in diffusion formulations, model scaling, and decoding has brought DLMs from specialized text-generation settings to increasingly capable general-purpose models. The next step is to translate these advances into strong performance and practical efficiency across demanding applications. Continuous text diffusion models established generation through denoising learned token representations. Diffusion-LM explored controllable generation, while DiffuSeq and DiffuSeq-v2 developed sequence-to-sequence diffusion and bridge between discrete corruption and continuous representations [16, 17, 27]. Alongside these models, D3PM formalized structured categorical corruption [3]. Reparameterized Discrete Diffusion Models (RDM) exposed routing interpretation of backward sampling [67]; SEDD and MDLM further developed discrete score modeling and masked-token reconstruction [31, 47]. Beyond text reconstruction, Diffusion of Thought explored denoising explicit reasoning trajectories [61]. Ye et al. [62] investigated discrete diffusion for planning and constraint-solving tasks, using multigranularity learning and adaptive generation order. These studies established capability directions that complement the development of general-purpose DLMs. Scaling made these ideas accessible through larger models. Adapting pretrained autoregressive checkpoints provided one route to diffusion language modeling [18]; LLaDA and Dream 7B broadened the publicly available model ecosystem [35, 64], and code-focused models such as Dream-Coder 7B 1 Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report extended masked diffusion to code generation and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards [19, 58]. Block diffusion combines sequential progress across blocks with parallel denoising inside each block [2]. Fast-dLLM and Fast-dLLM v2 developed complementary inference and adaptation techniques based on caching and confidence-aware parallel decoding [55, 56]. DreamReasoner further extends block diffusion to long chain-of-thought reasoning through block-size curriculum learning [57]. Industrial development now spans commercial systems such as Mercury and publicly released models such as DiffusionGemma and LLaDA2.2 [11, 22, 23]. These systems have expanded the scope and deployment options of diffusion language modeling. As the model ecosystem matures, agentic applications provide demanding test of this progress: they require both capable tool use and efficient generation through repeated interactions with an environment. Strong results on isolated reasoning or code-generation tasks do not by themselves establish reliable repository-level problem solving. Competitive agent performance remains challenge for open DLMs. Recent models already include agent evaluations, but the reproduced comparison shows that LLaDA2.2 flash and DiffusionGemma still trail the evaluated Qwen baselines on both Terminal-Bench 2.1 [32] and SWE-bench Verified [9]  (Table 1)  . Advancing agent capability while retaining efficient parallel generation is central motivation for Clover. To this end, we present Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, an efficient and capable diffusion language model designed for agentic applications. It combines 35B-total, 3B-active mixture-of-experts architecture with bidirectional adaptation of Gated Delta Networks. Completed context is represented by recurrent memory, while tokens in the active block interact through softmax attention. shared softmax combines historical and block-local information, with learnable block-size calibration and separate right-context convolution branch. Our evaluation emphasizes agentic coding and tool use alongside general capabilities, and examines the cost of turning parallel predictions into accepted output tokens. The report first introduces the modeling and decoding background, then presents Clovers architecture, benchmark results, and runtime analysis. Separate sections examine on-device deployment and decision-model variant that generates related answers jointly. We release model weights, supervised fine-tuning code, and the inference engine, with particular emphasis on dedicated infrastructure for running Clover locally on consumer devices. We will continue to improve inference speed and model performance, expand multimodal capabilities, and contribute to the continued development of diffusion language models.

sections.title: 5 Clover Decision Model
sections.content: Human decision-making is often described in terms of fast, intuitive System 1 thinking and slower, deliberate System 2 reasoning. Drawing on this distinction, Jev, commercial model from TypeSafe AI, targets fast, structured decisions that software can use directly [1]. This motivates the Clover decision model: we use block diffusion to produce related judgments jointly in single denoising pass, combining fast response with the ability to share information across decisions. 5.1 Joint decisions in one denoising step The Clover decision model is variant for fast, structured judgment tasks. Given shared material and set of questions, it predicts up to eight answers together in single denoising pass after context prefill. This variant is planned for subsequent release. Let 𝑐 denote the shared material and 𝑞1, . . . , 𝑞𝑀 the associated questions, with 𝑀 8. We place these in the input and provide fixed answer template in one diffusion block. Each question has one masked answer position, while the surrounding format is given. One denoising pass predicts all answer positions, and each prediction is read over that questions candidate labels. Independent mode instead . invokes the same model separately for each 𝑐, 𝑞 𝑗 ( ) All answer positions share the input and can exchange intermediate features within the block. This provides way to use related evidence across decisions: for example, several judgments about contract may depend on the same disclosure exception. The mechanism supports coordinated prediction, although single pass does not guarantee that the resulting answers satisfy every constraint. 14 Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report 5.2 Decision quality We compare joint and independent prediction using the same decision-model checkpoint on an internal set of 500 groups with 2,420 questions and set of 50 partially completed 4 4 Sudoku boards with 364 missing entries. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, 35B-total, 3B-active mixture-of-experts diffusion language model built around bidirectional adaptation of Gated Delta Networks. Its architecture combines recurrent historical memory, selective interactions within the current block, learnable block-size calibration, and bidirectional local features. The benchmark results show consistent lead across the evaluated agent metrics alongside competitive general capabilities, with opportunities for further improvement in knowledge and mathematics. Quantized deployment offers further direction for studying this architecture under memory constraints. Our decision-model results additionally suggest that jointly generating related answers can improve the correctness of complete set of judgments. The next priorities are to further reduce latency, characterize the qualitylatency trade-off under matched evaluation conditions, and strengthen quantized deployment. We are also extending Clover toward multimodal capabilities, informed by Dream-VL and Dream-VLA work on vision-language understanding and robotic action modeling [63], and extending the context length.
